> Part of [**BeeSignal**](https://beesignal.ai) — a pricing-research engine that runs conjoint studies with LLM-generated synthetic consumers.

A model that fits *too* well is not good news. It is a symptom.

I was running a choice-based conjoint study for a fictional B2B SaaS product (call it *Planwise*) inside [BeeSignal](https://beesignal.ai), the engine I built to run pricing research with LLM-generated synthetic consumers instead of recruited humans. Fifty synthetic respondents, sixteen choice tasks each, a clean multinomial logit at the end. The estimation came back looking spectacular:

| Signal | Value | What it should be |
|---|---|---|
| Pseudo-R² | **0.911** | ~0.2–0.4 for real conjoint |
| Standard errors | **0.000 on all 13 coefficients** | strictly positive |
| Willingness-to-pay | **up to $1,683 / seat** | tens of dollars |

A pseudo-R² of 0.911 on choice data is not "a great model." It is the statistical equivalent of a smoke alarm. And standard errors of *exactly* zero are impossible in any well-posed maximum-likelihood problem — they mean the optimizer never found a finite answer. This post is the post-mortem: three layers of investigation, from what the LLM actually said down to the geometry of the likelihood surface.

## The suspect: perfect separation

The hypothesis I started with was **perfect separation**. In a logit model, separation occurs when the data is perfectly linearly separable — when some linear combination of the features classifies every choice without error. When that happens, the log-likelihood keeps *increasing* as the coefficients march off toward $\pm\infty$. There is no finite maximum to converge to, so the optimizer stops at some large-but-arbitrary value, and the Hessian it reports there has collapsed toward zero. Since standard errors come from inverting that Hessian,

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat\beta) = \sqrt{\operatorname{diag}\big(\,[-H(\hat\beta)]^{-1}\big)},
$$

a singular Hessian produces standard errors that are numerically zero — and coefficient magnitudes that are physically meaningless.

The interesting question was *why* a synthetic-consumer study would separate when a human one wouldn't. My bet: **temperature**. I had run the LLM at `temperature=0.7`, low enough that each persona behaved almost deterministically — always picking the "obviously better" option, never wavering. Real survey respondents are noisy; that noise is what keeps the likelihood well-behaved. Remove it and the data becomes too clean to estimate from.

## Layer 1 — what did the LLM actually do?

First, the raw responses. Across 800 choices the split looked unremarkable — 53.4% chose option A, 44.5% chose B, 2.1% picked neither. But two things stood out:

- **Confidence was pinned to the ceiling.** Mean self-reported confidence was 0.90, with a 75th percentile of 0.95. The personas were almost never unsure.
- **Counterbalancing agreement was 86.6%.** Each task was shown twice with the options swapped (A/B → B/A) to catch position bias. When you re-ask a noisy respondent the same question with the order flipped, you expect disagreement a fair chunk of the time. Agreeing 86.6% of the time — at a temperature that is supposed to inject randomness — is the first fingerprint of over-determinism.

Suggestive, not yet damning. For the smoking gun I had to look at *consistency*.

## Layer 2 — the smoking gun

A conditional logit conditions on each respondent: it explains the choices *within* a person, using only the contrasts between the options they saw. So separation is a **within-respondent** property. The right question is not "do all respondents agree?" — they shouldn't, and they don't — but "is each individual respondent perfectly rationalizable by a single fixed utility ordering?"

Two measurements answered it:

- **Price monotonicity: 100%.** In all 650 tasks where one option was strictly cheaper, the cheaper option was chosen. Not 70%, not 85% — every single time.
- **Per-respondent consistency: 100% for all 50 respondents.** Each persona's sixteen choices were perfectly explained by one deterministic utility ranking, with zero internal contradictions.

That is exactly the data-generating process that breaks maximum likelihood. Every respondent's choices were *perfectly separable on their own*. Pool fifty perfectly-separable panels and the conditional likelihood has no finite maximizer. (Tellingly, the *pooled* per-attribute dominance rate was only ~55% — proof that the personas had genuinely different tastes. They weren't all picking the same thing; each was just internally, mechanically deterministic.)

## Layer 3 — the geometry of the failure

The estimation layer confirmed it cold. Inspecting the Hessian at the reported optimum:

| Diagnostic | Value | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Condition number | **2.94 × 10²⁰** | ≫ 10¹² → numerically singular |
| Rank deficiency | **8 of 13 eigenvalues ≈ 0** | likelihood is flat in 8 directions |
| Min eigenvalue | ≈ 0 (not > 0) | not positive-definite → no true maximum |

And the coefficients themselves gave the game away:

```
seats_100             β = +100.8        support_email    β = -45.2
seats_unlimited       β =  +84.7        support_dedicated β = +66.2
storage_unlimited     β =  +95.6        price            β =  -0.06
```

A well-identified conjoint has utilities in roughly the $[-3, +3]$ range. Coefficients of *one hundred utils* are not estimates — they are the optimizer sprinting toward infinity and getting cut off by an iteration limit. The near-zero price coefficient is what then detonates the WTP numbers: willingness-to-pay is $-\beta_\text{attr}/\beta_\text{price}$, so dividing a 100-util feature effect by a price coefficient of −0.06 yields the absurd $1,683.

The causal chain, end to end:

```
temperature = 0.7
  → personas near-deterministic (always pick the "obviously better" option)
  → every respondent's choices are perfectly separable on their own
  → conditional log-likelihood has no finite maximum (β → ∞)
  → Hessian → singular at the cutoff point
  → standard errors = 0
  → β_price → 0, feature β → 100  ⟹  WTP explodes
```

## The fix

The diagnosis dictated the remedy. The problem was never the model or the data pipeline — it was that the respondents had no noise. So you add it back, in calibrated amounts:

| Fix | Change | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Raise temperature** | `0.7 → 1.1` | restores realistic ~75–85% consistency, breaking separation |
| **More respondents** | `N = 50 → 100` | satisfies the Orme sample-size rule, shrinks SEs honestly |
| **L2 regularization** | `λ = 0.1` on the MNL | a guaranteed backstop: a ridge penalty makes the Hessian invertible even if some separation survives |

Temperature is the lever that matters most. Adding a small ridge penalty is the seatbelt — it bounds the coefficients and restores a finite, invertible Hessian regardless.

## Why I keep this notebook

The honest reason this study is worth writing up is that the failure is *specific to synthetic data* and easy to miss. With human respondents you essentially never see perfect separation, because people are gloriously inconsistent. Swap in an LLM at low temperature and you manufacture respondents who are too rational to estimate from — and the model rewards you with a pseudo-R² of 0.911 that looks like a triumph instead of an alarm.

The lesson generalizes well beyond pricing: **when you generate your own respondents, the noise is a modeling choice, not a nuisance.** A synthetic-data platform needs a diagnostic gate — separation checks, Hessian condition numbers, sane coefficient bounds — sitting between "the run finished" and "the result is trustworthy." A number that is too good to be true usually is, and the most valuable thing a model can do is tell you exactly *how* it broke.
